# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about how we're obsessed with completion. We finish books, finish projects, finish conversations with decisive periods instead of trailing ellipses. There's something satisfying about the full stop, the closed loop, the sense that something is *done*.

But I wonder if we're missing something in this relentless pursuit of finished-ness.

Some of my favorite things are unfinished. A half-built garden where you can still see possibility in empty spaces. A conversation with an old friend that gets interrupted—not ending, just pausing, ready to resume whenever. Sketches rather than paintings, rough drafts rather than polished essays. These things hold potential in a way completed work sometimes doesn't.

There's also something deeply human about incompletion. We're never finished becoming ourselves. Our relationships keep developing. Even our understanding of the past shifts as we grow. Maybe unfinished isn't a failure state but the natural condition of a life lived with attention.

I notice people feel most creative when they're not trying to finalize everything. Permission to make something incomplete, to leave rough edges, seems to unlock more interesting thinking than the pressure to produce polished answers.

Perhaps the real skill isn't completion at all—it's knowing when something is finished enough. When to let go not because it's perfect, but because it's ready. Because sometimes the best things we make are the ones we release while they're still becoming, still reaching toward something we can't quite see.
